items.title: Harold Tejada Charged in Doping Case, Netcompany-Ineos Move Collapses Before It Begins
items.author: ahood
items.content: The ITA charged Harold Tejada with an anti-doping violation over blood passport abnormalities. Netcompany-Ineos has called off the Colombian's 2027 transfer.
items.lbText:
Tejada was provisionally suspended Friday by the ITA. (Photo: Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP via Getty Images)

Netcompany-Ineos is dropping a transfer of Harold Tejada for 2027 after the International Testing Agency charged the Colombian climber with an anti-doping rule violation and provisionally suspended him.

The ITA said Friday it charged Tejada, 29, with using a prohibited substance or method after unexplained abnormalities in the blood values tracked by his Athlete Biological Passport .

An expert panel reviewed Tejada’s explanation and maintained that the abnormalities were “highly likely to have been caused by the administration of a prohibited substance and/or a prohibited method,” the agency said .

The ITA did not identify a specific substance or method, or disclose the dates of the passport data.

The agency imposed a mandatory provisional suspension under UCI rules. Tejada can challenge the suspension and request a hearing before the UCI Anti-Doping Tribunal.

Tejada said on Instagram that the ITA notified him on November 26. He said he had provided the information requested and that his legal and medical team would present his defense.

“I want to clarify that this suspension is a temporary measure and does not constitute a sanction or a final decision,” Tejada wrote . ( See full statement below ).

Netcompany-Ineos announced last month that Tejada would join the British squad for 2027, but the team posted a short message on X announcing that the deal is over.

“Netcompany INEOS and Harold Tejada have agreed to end their agreement for the 2027 season, before he was due to join the team on 1 January,” a note read.

Tejada has raced for XDS-Astana since 2020 and enjoyed a breakout 2026.

He won stage 6 of Paris-Nice, finished fourth overall at the UAE Tour, and hit 10th overall at the Vuelta a España. He also finished second on stage 13 of the Tour de France in Belfort won by Mauro Schmidt.

There was no immediate comment from XDS-Astana officials on Friday.

It’s the latest biological passport case to hit the men’s WorldTour since Oier Lazkano , who was provisionally suspended on October 31, 2025. That case remains unresolved.

To the public, cycling fans and everyone who has supported me throughout my career,

On November 26, 2026, the International Testing Agency (ITA), acting on behalf of the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), notified me that it had opened anti-doping disciplinary proceedings against me.

I am provisionally suspended pending the outcome of these proceedings in connection with an investigation into my biological passport.

I want to clarify that this suspension is a temporary measure and does not constitute a sanction or a final decision.

From day one, I have acted diligently and responsibly, promptly providing all the information requested of me. I will continue to do so throughout the process, with full respect for the anti-doping authorities and cycling’s governing institutions.

My legal and medical team will present my defense to the relevant bodies through the established channels.

Out of respect for the confidentiality of the proceedings, I will refrain from making any further statements while the case is ongoing.

I am deeply grateful to my family, my friends and everyone who has expressed their support over the past few days.

I respectfully ask for your understanding at this time and for you to respect our privacy.

items.title: Forget Pauline Ferrand-Prévot. She’s Pauline van Baarle Now.
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: 'I will be a little more Dutch': Former Tour de France Femmes and Paris-Roubaix winner takes Dylan van Baarle’s name after their recent wedding.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Francois LO PRESTI / AFP via Getty Images)

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot is taking a new name now that she’s married Dylan van Baarle .

And thankfully, it’s not “Pauline Ferrand-Prévot van Baarle.”

“I would like to be called Pauline van Baarle,” the 34-year-old superstar told NOS on Friday.

The rider who was “PFP” married fellow pro cyclist “DVB” last month in the Netherlands.

This first-ever marriage of two Paris-Roubaix champions marked the end of an era.

Pauline told NOS on Friday that her home French fans will have to suck up the loss of their affectionate PFP moniker and start practicing their pronunciation.

“I understand that it won’t be easy for everyone to pronounce, but for me and for Dylan, it is very important,” she said.

“I will be a little more Dutch next year,” she joked.

It’s all change for Pauline van Baarle next year.

The revelation of her new name came the very same day her team also took a new married identity.

The women’s team that was Visma-Lease a Bike became Rabobank-Lease a Bike on Friday after the Dutch bank stepped up to take co-title sponsorship of the squad.

Beyond that, PVB might be approaching the bike a little differently in 2027.

She explained in an Instagram post celebrating her wedding earlier this month that she’d endured a long period of self-reflection after she burned herself out preparing for her Tour de France Femmes title defense.

“It was an absolutely special day,” she wrote about her wedding. “I remembered being happy when winning the Olympics, Tour, or Roubaix. But this feeling of getting married to Dylan with the presence of the most important people in my life was another level of joy, happiness, and fulfillment.

“Experiencing this feeling of being so happy while not sacrificing everything or being extreme was something I never experienced before. On that last sentence I will take note for the future,” she wrote.

Au revoir , Tour de France-obsessed Pauline Ferrand-Prévot.

Hallo to the wedded, wiser Pauline van Baarle.

items.title: You Really Do Need 10 Percent More Calories for Winter Rides – Just Not All Carbs
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: A UCI review backs up why cycling in the cold burns more energy, and explains how to balance your macros and hydration when temperatures drop.
items.lbText:
There are more myths around fueling for the cold, bleak bike rides of winter than we can list.

But fear not – there’s no need to get bogged down in all of those. In fact, most of them are BS that can be ignored.

However, there is one nutrition myth cyclists should definitely listen to in the coming months.

Cycling in the cold is proven to be more metabolically demanding and more hunger-inducing than cycling in moderate conditions. In fact, a group of leading sport scientists suggested recently that athletes should eat an extra 10 percent, if not more, in the winter.

That’s timely news so soon after Thanksgiving.

Here’s why cyclists should respect their raging winter appetites, and why they can block out most of the other noise about cold weather nutrition.

There’s a reason why you’re always hungry after a frost-bitten bike ride. Studies have proven that cycling in the cold drives energy demand through the roof.

If your interval sessions suck when it’s cold out, that’s because winter really does make you weak.

Muscular performance has been shown to decline by as much as six percent with every degree centigrade dropped.

Tissues become less “elastic,” contractile speeds slow, and the nervous system becomes less efficient in “firing” the muscles.

This six percent theory was founded in studies on maximal dynamic force rather than endurance activities. However, it’s understood that similar implications apply to slow-twitch sports; maintaining the same workload with cold muscles is more demanding than with warm muscles.

Your mind isn’t playing tricks on you. Riding in the winter really is “harder” than riding in more moderate conditions.

Firstly, because cold air is dense air. This “thickness” increases a rider’s aerodynamic drag, possibly by as much as four percent for a 10-degree C dip in temperature.

This can cost around one kilometer per hour at speeds above 30kph, and make maintaining any target speed feel harder.

Secondly, the two sets of tights, three pairs of merino socks, and five upper layers you wear for your winter rides is not exactly a high-performance setup.

Every extra wardrobe item introduces friction to the system and increases energy demand.

Third and final point: Frost-bitten shivering costs energy and will further stoke the metabolic furnace.

According to six leading sports scientists who scoured dozens of studies as part of a recent UCI “ Sport Nutrition Project ,” training in winter is taxing enough to warrant an extra-large serving of your post-ride meal.

“Given the greater energetic demands of cycling in the cold, one consideration is to maintain energy balance by increasing daily energy intake, accounting for an estimated 10 percent increase in energy expenditure at moderate exercise intensities,” reads the UCI review .

All athletes will know that maintaining energy balance is crucial to training, recovery, and 24/7 health. The winter sickly season is the worst time for an athlete to stray into deficit, so take that 10 percent rule and enjoy it.

And remember – the UCI’s “10 percent increase” is just ballpark. If you’re sadistic enough to be smashing high-intensity rides when the mercury is far below zero, that “10” could become 15 or 20.

But don’t use the 10 percent allowance as an excuse to simply crush comforting, stodgy carbs.

The popular “widsom” that athletes oxidize more sugar or need more carbohydrate during winter is only partly true.

Those cravings for a bottomless bowl of oatmeal after a hard winter ride is a product of increased caloric demand rather than any metabolic “need.”

There’s still no definitive proof that the body increasingly relies on carbohydrates in winter, despite what your Insta feed might tell you.

Instead, split those extra calories across carbs, fats, and protein.

As the UCI says, “There is no need to adjust the percentage of carbohydrates or macronutrient composition. The priority should remain on maintaining overall caloric intake.”

So consider adding an extra spoon of peanut butter and some Greek yogurt to that bucket of oatmeal you’ve been dreaming of.

Everybody has a take on how to hydrate on a winter ride. And in many cases, those theories seem to conflict.

“Y ou should drink more because you sweat more in all the heavy layers .”

“ You should drink less because you sweat less in the cold .”

“ You should drink more because you lose water through the breath. ”

It turns out all of that is true, all at once.

The body loses more heat through convection in the cool and so becomes less dependent on sweat for thermoregulation.

However, it’s also not uncommon for riders to actually sweat more in winter as they slow-boil themselves beneath one too many insulating layers .

In some cases, the two things more or less balance out, albeit rarely. Every athlete has their own point of equilibrium, depending on the conditions and exercise intensity.

In general, athletes sweat less in winter unless they’re a notorious over-dresser.

However, hydration shouldn’t be neglected, even in the sub-zero.

Your body loses fluid in sneaky ways in the cold.

Cold air contains less water vapor than warm air. Your respiratory system humidifies this dry air on inhalation – at the cost of the body’s water reserve.

And that weird thing where you need to pee more when you’re inconveniently wrapped into tights and jackets – a phenomenon known as cold diuresis – further drains the body.

According to the nerds at Precision Fuel & Hydration, these often-unaccounted losses can add up to one or two liters per day.

This problem is compounded by the simple fact you’re probably not drinking enough when you train in the cold. Who wants to swig from an icy bidon when you can barely feel your face?

All this means that athletes should pay as much attention to fluids in winter as they do in more temperate conditions.…

items.title: Big Tech Is Ready to Exploit Garmin’s Clunky Software Problem
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: 24/7 biometrics, ride history and now TrainingPeaks give Garmin an advantage, yet missteps and an AI push from Apple and Google leave the lead far from guaranteed.
items.lbText:
Over the years, I’ve watched the major bike computer brands push out new head units and hardware, and I’ve seen that hardware become less and less important. At one point, the head unit was merely a display, and if you wanted structure, you pulled a copy of Joe Friel’s The Cyclist’s Training Bible off the shelf to guide your training. Then those devices gradually turned into data collection and display devices. Now the entire world has been turned upside down by AI, and somewhere along the way from step two to step three, the ecosystem—and later the data—became far more important than any hardware ever could be.

Today, Garmin, Wahoo, Coros, and Big Tech are all circling the same space, but Garmin has an edge. Garmin was the first to focus on the ecosystem and the company’s role as a repository of data rather than just a hardware company. It’s a walled garden, and while not everyone loves it, Garmin has somehow managed to keep most users pretty happy inside it. Now other brands are catching on, though, and Garmin is at a precipice. Is the company going to be able to turn the corner and go toe-to-toe with Big Tech, or will Garmin stumble right when it matters?

This is a mix of business strategy, technology, and a dash of the future of the world. I can’t get enough.

This all comes bubbling up because I handle the buyer’s guide for bike computers, and I think about this a lot. This isn’t a plug for the buyer’s guide, but I see my role as not just listing the specs for each bike computer—I’m trying to translate why you should spend your money with one brand over another. If I tell you to buy brand X today, I understand that could mean for the next 10 years you only buy computers from that brand. If that seems like I’m overthinking it, just think Wahoo versus Garmin and how many people absolutely refuse to consider the opposite of what they started with.

And with that in mind, I try to look at what you are really buying. Coros, Garmin, Wahoo, and Hammerhead all make quality bike computers that do the job. If you only want a CatEye from 2002, it doesn’t matter which one you pick—they all do that just fine. So what sets the different computers apart?

What has started to emerge is that you’re buying into an ecosystem, and Garmin recognized that long before anyone else with a series of strategic purchases. It started on the hardware side, buying power-meter pioneer MetriGear in 2010 and indoor smart-trainer giant Tacx in 2019. With those purchases and with the company’s own sensors, nearly every watt, heartbeat, and indoor session landed in Garmin Connect. Then, in 2020, Garmin acquired Firstbeat Analytics—the Finnish company behind the VO2 max, training load, and recovery algorithms that much of the fitness industry relied on—and turned that data into something actionable.

In the meantime, the other companies in this little pond have struggled to recognize the need. Hammerhead started with a push for a richer, more modern computer on the bars—promising that “the bicycle of the future will be intelligent and data-driven” and aiming to let riders “ignore your phone and ride.” It’s a position that makes sense, but it’s also an inherently hardware-focused position, and that is still reflected now that SRAM owns the company. Today it’s deeply embedded into the SRAM hardware ecosystem with a wealth of info about how people use their bikes, but it completely lacks a biometrics ecosystem to match.

Wahoo, on the other hand, seemed to be on the right track. The company dominates the indoor trainer market and has a solid hardware lineup of sensors and computers, plus structured workout tools that give riders guided sessions rather than just raw numbers. Still, it’s missing the continuous, 24/7 biometric and multi-sport data engine Garmin has built. Wahoo tried to fix that with a watch, but that failed spectacularly—and the training and analytics pieces have felt more bolted-on than seamless. It’s close in spots, but not quite there.

At least it wasn’t quite there until Coros broke onto the scene. Coros essentially duplicated the Garmin ecosystem—minus the smart trainers and power meters—putting the training pieces, bike computers, and watches under one roof for less money. The brand doesn’t have the cycling market in hand yet, but by partnering with Wahoo, both companies suddenly added missing pieces and really turned the corner.

Except that is playing catch-up. There’s still some friction between Coros and Wahoo, with some indications that the partnership may not last, but we can ignore that for now. Even if Wahoo and Coros put it all together perfectly, that only puts the two companies on equal footing with where Garmin already was. Garmin isn’t sitting still, though. This year, Garmin potentially jumped ahead again by buying TrainingPeaks and TrainHeroic—a move that could take all of this a step further by approaching the same data from the coaching side.

It’s not just the bike brands fighting over this space. Apple, Google, and Samsung have all been building out their own health and fitness ecosystems, and these companies are some of the biggest in the world. They come at the problem with resources that make a bike brand’s budget look like pocket change. Apple has HealthKit and Apple Health sitting right at the center of the iPhone and Apple Watch world, tying everyday vitals, sleep, and medical records into one hub while testing conversational health AI tools. Your iPhone can actually work as a somewhat credible bike computer when paired with an Apple Watch.

And on the Android side, there are challengers as well. Google has pushed deeper with Google Health and a Gemini-powered Health Coach that pulls together workouts, sleep, and broader health context, and Samsung has leaned into daily readiness scores, sleep vitals, and an AI health assistant across its watches and phones.…

items.title: Rabobank Replaces Visma on Women’s Jersey — No Confirmation Yet on Men’s Team
items.author: ahood
items.content: Rabobank returns as title sponsor of the women's WorldTour team but questions remain around the men's team in the latest shakeup at the Visma-Lease a Bike franchise going into 2027.
items.lbText:
Ferrand-Prévot and Vos, center, will race in Rabobank jerseys in 2027. (Photo: NICOLAS TUCAT / AFP via Getty Images)

Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot will race in Rabobank colors again in 2027, but the men’s Visma-Lease a Bike team name remains up in the air.

The squad will race as Rabobank-Lease a Bike Women’s Pro Cycling, the team announced Friday, after the Dutch bank steps back into the spotlight.

Visma is stepping away from naming rights of the Dutch franchise , and officials said Rabobank will keep its existing jersey space on the men’s and development squads as a partner.

That suggests that Rabobank will not take over the title sponsor of the men’s team, at least right now.

“Given our shared history, the return of the Rabobank name as a title partner is a special moment. It demonstrates Rabobank’s confidence in our team and in the future of women’s cycling,” said team manager Richard Plugge on Friday. “We are proud to build on that confidence together.”

With the women’s team’s future secure, questions still remain around what kit the men’s team will be racing in next season.

The Dutch team has been dripping out news all week.

Nike confirmed its return to cycling this week as a team partner, but suspense continues to grow as there’s still no confirmation yet who will take Visma’s place in the men’s team name.

The deal marks the return of Rabobank after nearly a decade away.

Vos and Ferrand-Prévot spent five seasons with the former Rabobank women’s team from 2012 to 2016. The French star returned to the team in 2025 after winning Olympic gold in mountain biking in Paris.

The Dutch bank is a longtime backer of pro cycling starting in 1996, but it pulled its name from the men’s team at the end of 2012 after the USADA report on Lance Armstrong and the U.S. Postal Service team. Other revelations within Dutch cycling hastened the bank’s exit from the men’s peloton.

The squad raced as “Blanco” during part of the following season as Plugge began rebuilding the franchise into one of today’s top operations.

Rabobank continued to back the women’s team through 2016, and returned to the pro peloton in July 2025 as a partner of Visma’s men’s, women’s and development teams.

“By taking on a greater role in women’s cycling, we are building on that momentum,” said Carlo van Kemenade, a member of Rabobank’s managing board.

The deal follows another major investment in women’s racing.

TotalEnergies signed a five-season deal with Demi Vollering’s FDJ squad from 2027 as it ends its backing of Netcompany-Ineos as well as the men’s second-tier squad that will race with a new sponsor next season.

In the U.S., Human Powered Health shifted its focus to its women’s WorldTour team after folding the men’s ProTeam at the end of 2023.

items.title: ‘They Ran Out of Time’: Why Artem Shmidt Left Ineos for NSN
items.author: ahood
items.content: The young American brings time trialing horsepower and a growing appetite for the northern classics after moving from Ineos to NSN Cycling in 2027.
items.lbText:
Shmidt, a winner at the Classique Dunkerque in May, is heading to NSN. (Photo: Luc Claessen/Getty Images)

America might have its next cobblestone beast in Artem Shmidt .

The young American got his first real taste of the punishing cobbles in 2026, and it left him hungry for more .

And he’s already hooked on racing in Belgium.

“I don’t think there’s a greater feeling in the world than going up Kwaremont for the third time in a bike race with thousands of people screaming at you with those passionate Belgian fans,” Shmidt said this week. “That was a quite incredible feeling.”

With a move from Netcompany-Ineos to NSN Cycling for 2027, Shmidt is hoping to find the freedom to chase more results and develop his skills on the pavé .

No American man has ever hoisted the cobblestone trophy in the Paris-Roubaix velodrome or won the Tour of Flanders .

It’s way too early to pile that sort of pressure on his shoulders, but Shmidt packs a big engine coupled with strong time trialing chops that promise a lot more.

Shmidt’s transfer to NSN comes at an important crossroads in his career . Many say that the second contract to confirm a spot in the WorldTour is often the most challenging for a young pro.

After cutting his teeth in the WorldTour with two full seasons with Netcompany-Ineos, the Georgian penned a three-year deal with NSN.

The arrivals of Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz grabbed the biggest headlines , but Shmidt fits into the younger more aggressive part of NSN’s recruitment class.

“The team reached out to me quite early, sometime in the spring, and I was pretty keen off the bat,” Shmidt said during a media call this week.

“By the time we got things figured out, it was probably around Tour time, I talked with Ineos out of respect for them. I wanted to let them know what was happening,” he said.

“I was talking to other teams, and you guys probably know that sometimes it takes a little bit long to get things done with Netcompany. They ran out of time, and I ended up signing NSN, which I’m super grateful for. I’m looking forward to it and can’t wait to get things started.”

At Netcompany, he was way down the pecking order. At NSN, he expects more freedom.

“I like to not have a leash on and just race aggressively,” Shmidt said.

Shmidt’s calendar for 2027 remains TBD, but he will keep building out his time trial skills and get another shot at the northern classics. Racing a grand tour is also on his wish-list.

At 6-foot-2 and 170lbs, some say he has a build like Fabian Cancellara or his ex-Ineos teammate Filippo Ganna. Everyone’s been telling him he’s made for the classics since he started racing as a junior.

“I really fell in love with the classics and growing up watching them,” he said. “Everyone kind of tells you already that you’re going to be a classics rider just based off my physique and everything. So I was already quite mentally prepared to be a classics rider and that racing style.”

Netcompany-Ineos gave him a full taste in 2026, from Omloop Het Nieuwsblad all the way through Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix. He was even thrown into Amstel Gold Race and La Flèche Wallonne.

There were no major results, but he came out the other side stronger and hungrier.

That cobblestone initiation in part led to his breakout first European pro win at the Classique Dunkerque in France in early May.

NSN took notice and was quick to chase his signature for the team’s 2027 rebuild.

“Artem Shmidt is one of the most exciting talents to come out of the U.S. in recent years,” said NSN manager Kjell Carlström. “A big objective for us is to continue facilitating that development and see just how far he can go in one-day and stage races.”

The American men’s peloton has produced Tour de France winners, world champions, and some of the best time trialists in the history of the sport, yet the cobblestone monuments remain elusive.

George Hincapie came close, finishing second at Paris-Roubaix in 2005 and third at the Tour of Flanders in 2006.

Tyler Hamilton’s victory at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2003 remains the lone American victory across any of the men’s five monuments.

Shmidt, 23 in January, seems destined to find his place in the northern classics.

He raced in Europe as a teenager and split his time as a junior between the Belgian Cannibal squad and the American Hot Tubes program before stepping up to the U23 ranks with Hagens Berman.

Netcompany-Ineos opened the door to the WorldTour as a stagiaire in 2024, and now NSN will give him even more freedom in his deal through 2029.

“My goal [at Ineos] was just to learn as much as possible, and now hopefully at NSN I can try to become the best version of myself,” he said. “I won in Dunkirk with the late attack. I like to race aggressively, not overthinking too many things, just racing off instincts. I think this is the perfect team for me to do that.”

The final frontier for American men’s cycling is on the horrendous cobblestones.

There’s room to write more history. The last top-10 by an American in the men’s Roubaix was Taylor Phinney with eighth in 2018, and Sheffield with sixth at Flanders in 2024.

Other U.S. riders, like Neilson Powless, Matteo Jorgenson, and Magnus Sheffield, have made some noise recently in the northern classics. Powless won Dwars door Vlaanderen in 2025 and was fifth at the 2023 Ronde, while Jorgenson won Dwars in 2024 and hit a top-10 at the Ronde in 2023.

Shmidt isn’t making any bold declarations about winning Flanders or Roubaix just yet.

For now, it’s about taking more chances and finding out what he can do when he’s off the leash.

items.title: You Can Now Buy a 28-Gram, CNC-Machined Titanium Dynamo Taillight—If You’re One of 30 Buyers
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Berlin-based Allygn upgrades its EdelMü rear light from aluminum to high-polished titanium while keeping the same German-made Busch & Müller electronics inside.
items.lbText:
Berlin-based component brand Allygn has released a limited-edition titanium version of its EdelMü dynamo taillight, swapping the standard model’s aluminum housing for CNC-machined titanium for an extremely limited initial run.

The point of this kind of titanium extravagance is obviously to look great, but it does also solve a problem. For riders building custom randonneuring, bikepacking or commuter bikes, dynamo lighting has always been an aesthetic mismatch. While SON’s Edelux headlights are a staple on handmade builds, rear dynamo lights tend to look like an afterthought. Allygn founder and Fern Bicycles framebuilder Flo Haeussler originally designed the EdelMü to close that gap, taking the proven German-made internals from a Busch & Müller Mü taillight and housing them in a small, machined barrel that echoes the look of the Edelux.

It’s a natural problem for Haeussler to solve, as it’s the stated driving force behind the brand. Allygn Components specifically aims “for a fully integrated bicycle design, where every part blends seamlessly into each bike’s overall concept, both functionally and aesthetically.”

Which is why, as good as the EdelMü is, the new titanium version goes even further. The design keeps that exact formula but upgrades the outer shell from 6061 aluminum to high-polished, CNC-machined titanium.

Inside, nothing changes from a functional standpoint. The light ships with standard 6V AC dynamo internals from Busch & Müller, complete with capacitors to keep the stand light illuminated when stopped at intersections. Allygn says the housing can also accommodate 5-15V DC Mü internals for riders running e-bike or battery setups. Small cutouts machined into the titanium body provide side visibility.

The light measures 30.2 mm long with a 20.6 mm diameter at the plastic holder, and Allygn lists the weight at 28 grams including the uncut wiring and M3 bolt. Hardware consists of black zinc-nickel-plated stainless steel M4 and M5 bolts.

Two mounting configurations are available: an M6 direct braze-on option for custom frames and a POM ring mount. The ring-mount version is designed to pair with the rear light mount from fellow Berlin outfit Drust Cycles. Framebuilders can also source braze-ons directly from Allygn.

The titanium EdelMü taillight retails for €150, or roughly $142 for U.S. buyers through Fern Bicycles after German VAT is deducted at checkout (before any applicable import duties). A bundle pairing the ring-mount light with a matching titanium Drust Cycles mount is also available for €185.

Because only 30 lights are included in this first batch, availability is tight. Riders and builders can order through the Fern Bicycles website or contact Allygn directly for more information.

items.title: Visma-Lease a Bike Just Lost a Title Sponsor – Here’s Why It Matters
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Visma-Lease a Bike confirms Visma is stepping down but will remain a partner as team hunts new finance to keep pace with Pogačar in the Tour de France arms race.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP via Getty Images)

Visma-Lease a Bike confirmed Thursday that the Visma IT company will step down as the team’s co-title sponsor in 2027.

But the brand isn’t leaving the team altogether.

Visma will instead be designated a “founding partner” next year. The team’s jerseys will feature logos of several Visma brands, and the business will continue to provide data and AI support.

The news marks a pivotal moment for the team of Jonas Vingegaard, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Sepp Kuss.

There’s an escalating Tour de France arms race on both the men’s and women’s sides of the peloton, and the Dutch team needs to keep pace.

It’s been known since February that Visma was looking to reduce its contribution to the team. V-LAB management has been campaigning for a new co-title partner ever since.

The confirmation of Visma’s self-relegation Thursday – just one day after the “Killer Bees” expanded their collaboration with Nike – clears the way for a new backer to step in.

The team has not yet revealed who that might be. However, reports suggest further news might surface as soon as this week.

Visma joined the Dutch team as a secondary sponsor in 2019 and took naming rights in 2024.

The partnership aligned directly with Visma-Lease a Bike’s acceleration to the front echelon.

Primož Roglič went head-to-head with Tadej Pogačar and UAE Emirates at the 2020 Tour de France before Vingegaard won back-to-back yellow jerseys in ’22 and ’23.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot was next to win the team a maillot jaune before Vingegaard completed his grand tour treble at the 2025 Vuelta a España and 2026 Giro d’Italia.

According to a team statement, Visma’s new designation as “founding partner” recognizes the role it played in the team’s development and its innovative, science-led approach.

“Visma believed in our ambitions when we started working together in 2019. Since then, we’ve shared moments we could only dream of back then,” said team CEO Richard Plugge.

“I’m grateful to everyone at Visma for the trust they’ve placed in us over the years,” Plugge said. “Having Visma stay with the team as a founding partner reflects what we’ve built together.”

Visma’s backstep comes at a point when the team is struggling to keep pace with an escalating Tour de France arms race.

After Jumbo-Visma dominated at the turn of this decade, Pogačar and UAE Emirates-XRG blasted onto the scene with a blockbuster bank balance that helped buy wild success.

Pogačar has gone on to own the maillot jaune since 2024.

Meanwhile, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Lidl-Trek, and Decathlon CMA CGM followed UAE’s lead with new backers, big budgets, and bigger signings.

On the women’s side, TotalEnergies-FDJ Suez went large with Demi Vollering.

It’s understood that Visma contributed around €20 million to Visma-Lease a Bike’s annual budget. The team was estimated to need a further €10 million on top of that to keep pace with its nouveau riche rivals.

Plugge told Feltet.dk this May during the Giro d’Italia he wasn’t in a sweat about filling a void worth €20 or even €30 million.

“The search is going well,” Plugge told Feltet about his quest for a new paymaster. “In my view, we are the biggest investment opportunity in cycling right now. A lot of brands and companies recognize that, which is positive for us.

“Together with our current partners, we have major plans for the years ahead,” Plugge said.

What the next step in Plugge’s plan looks like might become clear very soon.

items.title: ‘So Stupid’: Mads Pedersen Dumps on One of UCI’s Most Ridiculous Rules
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Cobblestone star blasts regulation that forces riders joining new teams to black out their new bikes before January 1. Better not ask his thoughts about sock height rules, then.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Christine POUJOULAT / AFP via Getty Images)

You can always rely on Mads Pedersen to say it how it is.

In his latest quotebomb, the cobblestone bruiser slammed UCI registration rules, deeming them “fucking ridiculous.”

Speaking in this week’s episode of his Lang Distance podcast, Lidl-Trek’s verbose Dane blasted regulation that forces riders moving teams to black out their new equipment until January 1.

“It’s crazy with these contracts, isn’t it? Why don’t they just run from November 1 or December 1?” Pedersen said.

“It’s fucking ridiculous,” Pedersen raged. “It’s so stupid.”

Best not to ask Pedersen’s thoughts about the sock height rules, then.

UCI legislation requires rider contracts to align with the calendar year, rather than the racing season.

That means that riders who hook up with their new teams at December training camps must wear their outgoing employer’s kit. They can ride their new team bikes, as long as they’re debranded.

For example, Primož Roglič was recently spotted at the NSN Cycling winter get-together wearing a Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe jersey. The Slovenian was riding what was clearly an NSN-issued Cube bike, albeit with some hastily taped-over logos.

Pedersen suggested to podcast co-host Jakob Egholm that a simple paperwork tweak would fix the farcical off-season ritual.

“The contracts don’t have to be any different,” Pedersen said. “You can just add a clause to the contract saying that if you change teams, you’re allowed to use your new team’s equipment from December 1 or from the first team training camp.

“It would be so easy to change the contracts,” he said. “Then there wouldn’t be any bullshit or riders not getting their salary in December because they’ve ridden a Ridley when they were supposed to ride a Trek.”

Sergio Higuita famously got himself in hot water with EF Education-Nippo at the end of 2021 for this very same “ bullshit.”

The EF team threatened to “fire” the Colombian in the November of his final contract year, and so deny him some salary, after he was seen brazenly pedaling around on a Specialized bike supplied by his new team, Bora-Hansgrohe.

This commotion over contract dates crops up every off-season.

All it takes is a glimpse of a duct-taped bike logo to trigger a rider into a rage.

The continued backlash has prompted the UCI to promise that contract start dates will be officially moved from January 1 to November 1.

UCI director of sport Peter Van den Abeele said at the end of 2025 that such plans are in the works. However, the revised regulation has not yet been implemented.
