items.title: ‘It’s Not Going to Be Just Sole Leadership’: Quinn Simmons Campaigns for Tour of Flanders
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: After helping Mads Pedersen at the Tour and riding into late-season form, the 25-year-old says Lidl-Trek needs two cards on the table to beat Tadej Pogačar, Mathieu van der Poel, and Wout van Aert.
items.lbText:
Quinn Simmons is angling to ride the Tour of Flanders, the American champion revealed to Velo .

After years of avoiding the cobbled classics, a return to the Belgian monument would be a shake-up for Simmons, who has gravitated towards the hillier monuments in recent years.

It would also be a shake-up for the Lidl-Trek classics squad, with Simmons dropping into a team that has been built around getting Mads Pedersen a monument victory for the better part of the last decade.

It would also be the first time that Simmons has ridden Flanders since his debut in 2022, when he didn’t finish.

“My first objective of the year will be Flanders,” Simmons told Velo in an exclusive interview in Tucson, Arizona. “I still haven’t got the full confirmation that I can go, but in my head that is the first goal.”

The shift in program for Simmons stems from two separate but equally important developments from the 2026 season for the 25-year-old all-rounder.

“When I basically gifted Mads [Pedersen] a Tour stage this year, I think that was when the team started to realize that maybe there’s going to be some changes. For next year, it’s not going to be just sole leadership,” Simmons said.

“If that’s hard for him to accept, that’s how it is. For sure, he’s one of the best riders in the world, but now, with the team we have, we can’t only be putting eight guys around one anymore,” he continued.

“I think it’s not just for myself, but for the other riders we have on the team like [Mathias] Vacek and some other guys coming up. If we go into the monuments, you have to play with two cards. Pogačar, Van der Poel, and Van Aert—they’re too good to only beat with one. We’re gonna need to adapt that plan a bit.”

That confidence was gained not just through the Tour, where Simmons was a frequent attacking and pulling presence, but also through a successful one-day race campaign to end the year.

The high point was the Team USA win at the UCI World Championships with Brandon McNulty, but that was part of a bigger picture where Simmons showed his form throughout the Canadian, Italian, and Japanese races on his program.

He also has Remco Evenepoel as an example of how parachuting into Flanders can fit into a larger calendar.

“It came from how I was racing the one-day races at the end of the year,” Simmons said. “With the way Remco did it, where you do Catalonia first and then go to Flanders, I think it can work. If I can do an altitude block and then come to Flanders quite in good shape.

“If I have to be in Belgium the four weeks before, I just don’t believe I can maintain the form that I need that long, but I think if I can climb with a similar level to Worlds, I believe Flanders has at least the potential for something to happen.”

Simmons began his career as a highly touted classics prospect but quickly moved away from the cobblestones and toward the hill classics and the Tour de France.

While a return won’t change his ultimate goal of a Tour stage win, it does add another chance for Simmons and his Lidl-Trek team to win the big monument they have been lacking.

“If I can be there in the same role there, that’s how Mads [Pedersen] can win—if we go there together,” he said. “Hopefully that gets approved, and if not, then I’ll just do my normal program of going to Basque, Amstel, and then preparing for the Tour.”

items.title: How the Giro Women Saw Viral Acclaim for Harrowing ‘Elimination of Violence’ Campaign
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Giro d'Italia women's and men's races break the mold by using their sporting platforms to highlight difficult societal issues others might avoid.
items.lbText:
The Giro d’Italia Women and men’s Giro d’Italia blew up Instagram on Wednesday with a post calling out violence against women.

The collaborative post has become one of the most “liked” pieces of content on both profiles and has drawn debate and acclaim across the sport.

The Instagram gallery features a series of juxtaposing images.

The road rash and scuffed knees of racing are paired with harrowing photos of women with black eyes, bloodied knuckles, and bleeding noses.

Each slide features a pair of related captions.

“I slipped – but I know how to get back up” / “I slipped – and I can’t find a way out” is one example.

The final slide and post caption urge better awareness and policing of violence against women.

“No woman should have to hide behind such different stories behind the same words. No woman should ever have to live through something like this,” reads the closing note.

The post Wednesday marked the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.

November 25 was designated a day to raise awareness that women are subjected to rape, domestic violence, and other forms of abuse by the United Nations General Assembly.

The Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women were among the very few sporting outlets to use their platforms to recognize the campaign.

By contrast, International Women’s Day in March is met annually with (potentially tokenistic) content from stakeholders across world sport.

The Giro d’Italia Women has since been hailed by key figures across professional sport for its proactive, provocative use of its global reach.

Time trial world champion Marlen Reusser, TV pundit and journalist Orla Chennaoui, and the men’s Quick-Step team are among the hundreds to have shown support.

Key figures in athletics, ultramarathon, and Formula 1 also commented.

“It’s so easy for any female brand or gender-neutral brand to jump on a bandwagon when the messaging is convenient,” Chennaoui said in a separate reel commenting on the Giro’s post. “It is so easy to speak up for women on International Women’s Day. In fact, in many cases, it’s detrimental not to.

“Where you see authenticity and where it really matters is when nobody is looking on a random Wednesday morning, and you’re then shouting out in support of and in defense of vulnerable women,” Chennaoui said. “That’s when it matters.”

The Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women entered a new chapter earlier this year when Luca Guercilena took over as general director of both races.

Guercilena was the long-time general manager of team Lidl-Trek.

The veteran Italian came to his headlining role at RCS Sport this September promising a forward-thinking approach to a very traditional sport.

Guercilena is already hinting at new race dates, formats, and concepts for the historic men’s Giro d’Italia. A progressive approach to social media might be another part of his regimen.

items.title: SBT GRVL and Rez Gravel Reach Agreement—Here Is What It Actually Means
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: A joint statement closes a 10-day dispute over the GRVL name, with major implications for both the Indigenous-led Arizona ride and SBT GRVL’s trademark defense.
items.lbText:
The controversy around the GRVL trademark has been resolved. Ten days after the issue came to a head, SBT GRVL and Rez Gravel released a joint statement confirming that the Indigenous-led ride can continue to use the GRVL term in its marketing.

The conflict started when Rez Gravel went public with an email the event received from SBT GRVL, notifying it of its trademark of the term GRVL. The post drew widespread attention on social media, with many commenters supporting Rez Gravel and criticizing the GRVL trademark in general.

Now, the dispute is settled. While the full text of the agreement has not been made public, Rez Gravel is permitted to use the GRVL term across its marketing and promotion in perpetuity, with no requirement to change its branding or anything associated with the event going forward.

“SBT GRVL and Rez Gravel are glad to share that we’ve resolved this matter and are moving forward on good terms,” the joint statement read. “After talking things through, both organizations have agreed that Rez Gravel will continue operating under its current name and branding, including REZ GRVL.

“Each organization understands the importance of protecting the brands we’ve built and respects the work the other has put into their respective events. We share a commitment to support the growth of gravel cycling and the communities that make this sport so special.”

In our conversation with SBT GRVL last week, the organization said its intention all along in the email was to reach an understanding with Rez Gravel over the use of the GRVL term. Under U.S. trademark law, trademark holders are required to actively police their marks; allowing unauthorized use to go unchecked can weaken a trademark or render it unenforceable in future disputes. Putting a formal agreement in place satisfies that requirement by establishing that Rez Gravel’s use is explicitly authorized rather than unpoliced.

Following the resolution, Amy M. Charity, founding partner and CEO of SBT GRVL, provided additional comments on the agreement and the event’s position.

“To us, GRVL has always represented so much more than four letters,” Charity said. “It’s about bringing people together, creating welcoming experiences and growing the cycling community. We share many of those same values with Rez Gravel, and we’re genuinely happy to have found a path forward that respects what we’ve each built. We fully support their continued use of GRVL and look forward to seeing their event and community thrive.”

Charity also pointed to SBT GRVL’s size and history with the event. “As a founder of SBT GRVL, this is deeply personal to me,” she said. “We’re a small, four-person business, and we’ve spent the better part of a decade pouring our hearts into creating an experience that people have come to know, love and look forward to year after year. My hope is that something really positive comes out of this and that the cycling community continues to rally around Rez Gravel and support the meaningful work they’re doing.”

Update: Shortly after this story was originally published, Rez Gravel responded to an earlier request for comment from Velo with the following statement:

“Per the agreement with SBT, which I cannot disclose, I’m glad that the matter between the Parties has been resolved, that Rez Gravel continues to use its name and branding, including REZ GRVL, that no money changed hands, and that neither Party admitted any wrongdoing.”

Prior to the joint statement, the organization had indicated that an agreement was in the works, posting on Instagram on November 19 to state its commitment to retaining the GRVL distinction.

Because the agreement grants Rez Gravel perpetual permission to use the mark—and formally documents that consent—the arrangement settles the question for future editions of the Arizona ride while keeping SBT GRVL’s broader trademark defense intact.

items.title: How Primož Roglič Went From the Brink of Retirement to Signing With NSN in Days
items.author: ahood
items.content: Primož Roglič was a lot closer to retirement than everyone thought: How weeks of soul-searching and one decisive meeting sealed the deal within days.
items.lbText:
Roglič agonized over his decision whether to retire or not. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Primož Roglič spent weeks agonizing over whether to retire before needing just a few days to hammer out a deal to join NSN Cycling .

Roglič was off-contract with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe this year, and despite a slew of rumors that he was talking with other teams, just a few weeks ago, he still didn’t know if he’d be racing in 2027.

Speaking from his new team’s training camp in Spain, the 37-year-old admitted the biggest decision wasn’t which team to race for in 2027, but whether to race at all.

“Obviously, it took a while. It took a while definitely for me to figure it out, and then after the season, what to do, in which direction to go,” Roglič said on a call Wednesday.

“And the thing was that, the more I was thinking, the more I didn’t know actually what to do. So at the end, I really needed to let it go to look from a bit of a different perspective at some things.”

After reports of several deals falling through , Roglič revealed coming into November, he still didn’t know if he’d be racing.

But once NSN reached out, things moved quickly.

Roglič met with NSN’s manager Kjell Carlström, coach Paulo Saldanha, and sport director Steve Bauer less than two weeks ago, and within days, one of the biggest surprise transfers of the winter was sealed.

“And when I come in touch with NSN, I had a meeting with a couple of guys. Then it went super fast,” Roglič said. “Then in a couple of days, we signed because I get the belief and trust of the people, support, and, yeah, that was it, and that was enough.

“And the name itself, ‘Never Say Never,’ helped even more. So, yeah, three days later I was here in a team camp.”

It’s the latest twist in Roglič’s unique and sometimes unconventional pro racing career.

A former ski jumper, he didn’t turn pro on the road until mid-20s. Just when it looked like he was poised to rule the Tour de France, Tadej Pogačar shows up.

After three years with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, when he won a record-tying fourth Vuelta a España, the arrival of Remco Evenepoel meant he was the odd man out.

Roglič was overlooked for the Tour de France, so he wanted to go out with a bang. But then disaster struck just weeks before the Vuelta a España.

“I was hit by a car and I was not sure of going to Vuelta. I went all in to make myself ready. I was there. Then I want to win,” Roglič said. “I still got some good results toward the end of the season.”

Roglič was torn from walking away from cycling while he was still capable of winning at the highest level. Second at the Vuelta and a win at the European time trial championships proved he’s still near the sharp end of the peloton.

But he said he still loved the thrill of racing.

Roglič agonized day and night trying to decide if he wanted another season in the WorldTour.

“There are two sides,” he said. “You want to finish when you choose and when you’re on top. On the other, I’m still attracted to cycling. I like to compete.”

So what did NSN offer Roglič that convinced him to sign on the dotted line?

“And at the end, it came to the things or the basics that I would appreciate the most,” he said. “A trust, belief and support from the team.”

There are unconfirmed reports that Roglič took a haircut on his salary, but NSN Cycling did not reveal financial terms of the one-year deal.

Roglič’s late-hour arrival at NSN’s winter camp means no one yet has a clear idea of what his 2027 racing calendar might look like.

The Giro d’Italia’s proximity to Slovenia appeals to him, but so does a return to the Tour after missing out in 2026. And there’s always the prospect of another crack at the Vuelta.

“First things first,” Roglič said. “I need to get to know 150 people, learn the bikes, the equipment. Then we’ll start to make a more detailed program.”

NSN brass will be hoping to squeeze out one good season from Roglič’s legs as the team needs a strong 2027 to solidify the team’s ranking going into the next three-year WorldTour cycle. It ended 2026 ranked 19th, one spot out of the WorldTour guarantee.

One unexpected bonus of the move is teaming up with longtime grand tour rival Richard Carapaz, part of an ambitious transfer class that also includes Santiago Buitrago, American Artem Schmit, and Lennert Van Eetvelt.

“I’m especially happy to be in the same team because we were racing against each other our whole life,” Roglič said. “I’m his fan. I like the way he races, the way he deals with some things or the way he’s doing it. I mean it will be even nicer if we can achieve some good results together for this team.”

And will 2027 be the final act of the Primož Roglič show?

“We start with this one,” he said. “Let’s start and we see how we go and where we go.”

items.title: Nike is Coming Back to Pro Cycling
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Nike teams up with Visma-Lease a Bike and Nimbl in its biggest step back toward the peloton since partnerships with US Postal and the Tour de France.
items.lbText:
The iconic Nike Swoosh will return to the pro peloton in 2027.

Team Visma-Lease a Bike revealed Wednesday that Nike will collaborate with its current kit supplier Nimbl in an R&D arrangement that hints there’s more to come from the U.S. superbrand.

Starting next year, superstar riders like Jonas Vingegaard, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Sepp Kuss will wear kits manufactured by Nimbl but featuring both Nike and Nimbl’s logos.

A Visma-Lease a Bike statement Wednesday suggested all parties will benefit from what could be a landmark moment for Nike, and for pro cycling.

“Nimbl brings its expertise in materials, fit and customization, while Nike Cycling supports development with its expertise in innovation and design,” reads the note.

“The expanded partnership brings together the team’s elite racing insight with sport science and athlete-performance expertise from across Nike. It gives Team Visma-Lease a Bike, Nimbl, and Nike Cycling more opportunities to develop and test new ideas together under the conditions in which the riders compete,” it says.

The three-way collab will mark Nike’s biggest move in cycling in 15 years.

The humungous sportswear brand famously provided race kits for the U.S. Postal and then Radio Shack teams through the peak EPO era, and boasted a personal deal with Lance Armstrong.

Nike also sponsored the yellow, green, white, and polka dot jerseys of the Tour de France from 1996 through 2011.

However, the Portland powerhouse has kept its Swoosh outside the peloton since then, except for occasional shoe collabs.

Visma used special Nimbl x Nike cycling shoes during stages of both the Giro d’Italia and Tour de France in 2026, and Mark Cavendish often wore Nike-branded race kicks before he retired.

Nike also currently supplies Visma-Lease a Bike and women’s superteam FDJ United Suez with off-bike apparel, and has collaborated with Nimbl on two limited clothing ranges.

The expanded Nike deal comes at a key moment for Visma-Lease a Bike.

The Dutch team is hunting for a new backer, and its men’s division is struggling to keep pace with Tadej Pogačar and his UAE Emirates-XRG juggernaut.

Visma boss Richard Plugge suggested Wednesday that Nike could be crucial to the team’s future.

“We set a high standard for everything that helps us win, and that includes our kit. Nimbl is a specialist that shares that ambition. Bringing Nike Cycling’s expertise and creativity into the partnership opens up new possibilities for us,” Plugge said.

“Few brands have done as much as Nike to bring sport and athletes to a global audience. We’re proud to bring that experience into our partnership with Nike Cycling and take this next step together,” Plugge said.

“We want to build something together that moves both our team and the sport forward.”

There’s been speculation that Nike has been plotting a wider return to the pro peloton since it opened its apparel partnerships with Visma-Lease a Bike and FDJ United-Suez.

Speaking at the 2026 Tour de France, Nike project manager Kieran Ronan told WielerFlits that the brand isn’t ruling out a major return to bike racing.

With revenue of more than $50 billion a year, it would be one of the sport’s biggest brands.

However, Ronan said the consumer market comes first. Nike hasn’t made its own mass-market cycling kit since 2008.

“Everything is open for discussion at the moment,” Ronan said this summer. “The primary focus right now is on our return to this sport.

“We are closely monitoring professional cycling, but we are not losing sight of the needs of the recreational cyclist,” Ronan told Wielerflits . “We want to passionately provide them with the very best products. It is absolutely our ambition to play a major role in cycling again.”

Nike bulldozed into the world of trail and ultra running this year with its rebooted All Conditions Gear line and a swathe of high-profile team and race partnerships. Ten months later, Nike ACG is one of running’s hippest, most advanced clothing and trainer brands.

A play for the lucrative bike clothing market – a world where weekend warriors are willing to pay $200 for a jersey – might be next.

items.title: Riccardo Riccò Fires Back After Tadej Pogačar’s Ice Cream Quip About Doping
items.author: ahood
items.content: Tadej Pogačar joked that riders who dope could end up selling ice cream. Riccardo Riccò, banned for life and now running a gelato shop, fired back.
items.lbText:
Riccò, inset, reacted to some recent comments from Pogačar about 'selling ice cream.' (Photo: Gruber Images/Getty Images)

Tadej Pogačar didn’t name Riccardo Riccò outright in recent comments about doping in sport, but the banned-for-life ex-pro took it as a dig anyway.

Speaking to La Gazzetta dello Sport , Pogačar responded to a question about overnight anti-doping controls during this year’s Tour, when he and Jonas Vingegaard were among riders tested in the early hours before stage 15.

“Yes, you can be sure of it, doping does not exist now for the majority of the peloton,” Pogačar told La Gazzetta . “And besides, many want to stay in the environment even after the end of their careers, as sports directors, coaches … With one mistake, you risk ending up selling ice cream or something like that. No, the vast majority of the peloton would never do it.”

Pogačar didn’t name names, but Riccò — who runs ice cream shops in Italy — was quick to respond in an Instagram Story (now disappeared from his feed).

“I accept the dissing. It’s very funny. I’m up for the game. I actually expected it a lot sooner,” Riccò said in a video post in Italian, translated by Domestique .

“I have to say that it only takes a moment to end up making ice cream with me. So before talking, you’ve got to be 100 percent sure. I’ve seen a lot of people pass to the other side.”

Nicknamed the “Cobra,” Riccò has a lengthy doping rap sheet.

Riccò was riding for Saunier Duval when he tested positive for CERA at the 2008 Tour de France, after winning two stages. He was booted from the race, and the team pulled out. He later received a 12-year suspension after a 2011 blood transfusion, and Italy’s anti-doping tribunal banned him for life in 2020.

Mauro Gianetti, who managed Saunier Duval at the time and now leads UAE Emirates-XRG, told L’Équipe this summer that he had made mistakes in recruitment but denied responsibility for doping by his former riders.

Riccò, now 43, runs two gelato shops in Italy and organizes amateur cycling coaching and training camps.

Pogačar’s latest remarks were among his most candid on doping in the modern peloton.

“We race with heart and with the right mentality. We all know that prohibited, banned substances can damage your health. And, at the same time, cycling is a sport and nobody wants to risk their life for it,” he told La Gazzetta .

“Obviously, there will always be someone who tries to take a shortcut,” he said. “I have met so many riders over these years, and everyone loves cycling, the sport. Everyone dedicates 100 percent of their life to it; they commit to having proper nutrition, to preparing well. The coaches are good, there is a focus on recovery and we work tremendously hard.

“Nobody wants to risk losing all of this — it’s not worth it. We riders live for the sport in the right way and there is no desire to ruin ourselves.”

Pogačar is enjoying his final days of the off-season before joining his UAE teammates at a training camp in Spain.

items.title: These Are the Biggest Changes Coming to Pro Cycling in 2027
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Mega transfers, more Chinese bikes, and a UCI review that could upend bike design: These are all the changes you actually need to know about and why they matter.
items.lbText:
Big changes are coming to pro cycling in 2027, and we aren’t talking about Tadej Pogačar not wearing a rainbow jersey.

Tour de France hopefuls are making daring transfers.

Long-time backers are switching allegiances.

Races will be in different places, teams will have unwieldy new names, and the UCI will have implemented more rules when competition restarts in January.

A lot has changed in the world of pro cycling in the past few months – some things more important than others.

We’re not going to list every tiny tweak that’s been made to the pro peloton this off-season. Nobody wants to read that, not even us nerds at Velo HQ.

Instead, here are the changes for 2027 that you really need to know about – the ones being debated at every group ride and that will drive the narrative into the future.

Last year’s transfer window was wild. Remco Evenepoel and Demi Vollering both made moves that transformed their new teams’ futures.

There have been some similarly seismic transfers this winter – particularly in the women’s peloton.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Paula Blasi – two of the few women who might dethrone Queen Demi – both made blockbuster moves in the quest for the yellow jersey.

Meanwhile, Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig is looking for a career reboot with her “home” team, Uno-X Mobility, and the wildly underrated Cédrine Kebaol is jumping on the SD Worx-Protime juggernaut.

Niewiadoma’s move to Lidl-Trek will thrust the women’s team from relative anonymity into Tour de France contention. Blasi’s decision to team up with Marlen Reusser will elevate Movistar to a superteam on-par with FDJ and SD Worx.

Expect a shift in the Women’s WorldTour hierarchy next year.

The shakeup on the men’s side has been similarly huge, albeit maybe less transformational.

First up – no, Paul Seixas is not leaving Decathlon CMA CGM, yet .

Instead, NSN Cycling Team took the spotlight by landing the two biggest male transfers of the winter – Primoz Roglič and Richard Carapaz.

These ageless wonders won’t be worrying Pogačar in 2027, but they could bring NSN grand tour top-fives, countless stage wins, and endless entertainment.

A team that scrapped for stage wins with little success in 2026 will be a factor in 2027.

The success of Roglič’s season could also dictate how long he sticks in pro cycling. Will 2027 be Rogla’s last dance?

Felix Gall’s move to Lidl-Trek will be equally intriguing. Can the Austrian jump from the lower steps of stage-race podiums with a Lidl-Trek team that’s already bloated with wannabe grand tour winners?

If you’re still calling Jim Ratcliffe’s team “Ineos Grenadiers” and thought Michael Matthews rides for “Mitchelton Scott,” we’ve got bad news.

A slew of new team names is coming to pro cycling in 2027.

Quick-Step is out. After 24 years of cobbles and swagger, the very-Belgian flooring brand is done with bikes.

Instead, The Wolfpack will become Soudal-Safety Jogger in 2027 after the burly boot ‘n’ workwear brand stepped up as co-title partner.

Now that’s a name that’ll take some getting used to.

That said, it’s a refreshing blue-collar throwback to when the peloton was powered by everyday superstores, obscure farming equipment , and carpet brands.

On the flipside, brace for a bunch more obscure tech, finance, and IT companies placing their names inside pro cycling in 2027.

Canyon-SRAM is diving into investment and trading in partnership with Scalable Capital after its recent experiment with the Zondacrypto exchange ended in disaster .

Meanwhile, the team once known as TotalEnergies has been rescued by title sponsorship from Xefi, one of those IT brands that does business things you don’t really understand.

On that note – watch out who you call TotalEnergies in 2027.

TotalEnergies has totally withdrawn from the men’s peloton ahead of 2027 so it can go all-in on a long-term deal with the newly named TotalEnergies-FDJ United. As a reminder, the oil giant also terminated its non-naming deal with Netcompany Ineos .

In the long-term, TotalEnergies’ pivot could mark a tipping point for women’s cycling – it will be one of the biggest backers in the Women’s WorldTour and is committed for five years.

In the short term, it contributes another confusing team name to remember.

Sorry Bianchi fans, there won’t be any celeste in the pro peloton in 2027.

Bianchi’s problems extended from its year-end accounts to its stake in professional sport this autumn when Bahrain-Victorious dropped the historic Italian brand in favor of Factor.

As an aside while chatting cult brands with financial fears – Rapha is coming back to bike racing with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe.

The other headline in terms of bike sponsorship?

The Shandong-based manufacturer Pardus will join XDS in the premier cycling calendar in a blockbuster three-year deal with Xefi (that’s the team that was TotalEnergies, remember).

Pardus’ entry into elite cycling continues a paradigm shift in team-bike partnership.

The Chinese giant XDS blazed a trail by partnering with Astana in 2025 and then Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskada in 2026. Guangdong brand Quick-Pro followed suit with Euskaltel Euskadi in 2026.

Pardus is the next Chinese manufacturer looking to disrupt the Western-centric lockdown on pro cycling.

Heritage brands like Bianchi should take note – China is coming, fast.

One established Western manufacturer that needn’t be worried?

Yes, the behemoth U.S. manufacturer has split from the Quick-Step franchise after 18 years , but that’s because it’s so busy with three superteams from different corners of the sport: Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, TotalEnergies-FDJ United, and Specialized Off-Road.

The men’s and women’s Vueltas are on the move, USA loses out, and the world championships will be premature in the 2027 race calendar.

USA loses one of its marquee UCI-rated races. The Maryland Cycling Classic is shuttering for good.…

items.title: ‘We Were in Over Our Heads’: Inside the Wild Debut of America’s New Pro Cycling Team
items.author: ahood
items.content: Modern Adventure Pro Cycling won five races in its inaugural season. Bobby Julich explains how the team's bet on overlooked riders paid off and what's next for 2027.
items.lbText:
Oliver's big wins were the highlight of Modern Adventure's inaugural season. (Photo: DAVID PINTENS / Belga / AFP via Getty Images)

Modern Adventure Pro Cycling bet on a bunch of overlooked and undervalued riders in its first season, and came away with five wins and a world title on the track.

That’s according to coach Bobby Julich , who told Velo’s Hannah Gross at El Tour de Tucson that the inaugural season for America’s new cycling team delivered some sweet highs and a few gut punches .

Nothing was certain in the first major American men’s pro team in decades , but race organizers noticed how the riders stuck together on the roughest days.

“Everywhere George and I went, it was compliments of, ‘hey, you guys not only just showed up but you represented,’” Julich told Velo . “Yes, we were in over our heads quite a bit, but the guys rode together as a team. They fought together as a team, they enjoyed each other’s company, and we’re only going to get better from here.”

Julich said that sense of collective mission carried the team across 2026.

There’s a feeling of mission accomplished from season one .

Coming into the team’s winter camps, Julich said the momentum is already building for what everyone expects to be an even bigger 2027.

At the beginning of the year, co-founder George Hincapie described his team as a bit like the “Bad News Bears” of cycling.

The sport directors and staff stitched together a 21-rider roster this year based on riders who Julich said “fell through the cracks.”

“They’ve been told that they’re not good enough or they’re never going to make it, and then they come to our team,” Julich told Velo . “We supported them and gave them the confidence that it takes and the support that it needs. And they just blossomed.”

That sense of being underdogs and something to prove drove them across their first season.

Julich recounted a key moment early in the year when Mark Stewart, a journeyman from Scotland, expressed what it meant to the riders to be a part of the team.

“And he looked around the room, and he looked at me straight in the eye, and he said, ‘What you see here is seven of the most supported, confident, and happy people that we’ve ever been,’” Julich said. “That set the tone, that set the standard, and from there, even in races where we got slapped around pretty good, those guys stuck together.”

The results came. Stefan de Bod finished fourth overall at the AlUla Tour in the team’s first race, just 25 seconds off the win.

Five of its seven starters made it to the velodrome at Paris-Roubaix, including 23-year-old Cole Kessler.

Ben Oliver, a former mountain biker who finally earned a real wage racing bikes, won two stages and the overall at the Ethias Tour de Wallonie, a 2.Pro stage race in Belgium that gave the team its biggest success of the year.

Riley Pickrell delivered one more win to close out the road season at the Tour de Langkawi.

By October, Stewart won the points race at the UCI track worlds in Shanghai.

“For us as a first-year organization to have one of our riders win a world championship in any discipline is massive,” Julich said.

For season two, the team is upping its ambitions.

The team will race as Modern Adventure Factor Racing, with the bike brand stepping up as co-title sponsor to help the team’s goal of reaching the Tour de France within five years.

Modern Adventure brings on four new riders for 2027, and since everyone was signed to two-year deals, the roster jumps from 21 riders to 25 .

Modern Adventure adds WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch, sixth at Paris-Roubaix in 2025, from Lotto Intermarché, and reigning Australian road champion and WorldTour giant-killer Patrick Eddy from Team Brennan.

The team also signs New Zealand climber Josh Burnett from Burgos Burpellet BH, and Owen Cole, the 2023 U.S. U23 road champion and 2026 Tour de la Guadeloupe winner, from Team Winston Salem-Flow.

“We don’t yet have the pressure of getting UCI points or to get in the WorldTour,” Julich told Velo . “That’s a year or two further down the road that we have to start worrying about that.”

For 2027, it’s all about building on its first season and targeting even better results.

The team has yet to pin down its racing calendar, but it’s already confirmed for the Tour Colombia, which run January 26-31. The team is hoping to broaden its spring classics campaign to get into some of the hillier Ardennes-style one-days.

A grand tour is still a dream, but the team must hit the top-30 in the world team rankings before it qualifies. Modern Adventure ended 2026 ranked 36th, so inching up the rankings will start to matter going into 2028 if the teams wants a grand tour bid.

“What I learned the most is that when you get good people, passionate people, working together, regardless of their experience, that you’re going to have fun and be successful,” Julich said. “What we want to do in the future is just build upon what we did this year.”

items.title: Haro Files for Bankruptcy After the BMX Brand’s Short Foray Into Drop Bars
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Chapter 11 follows a $2.86 million lawsuit from supplier Kenstone, U.S. layoffs, and the brand handing its drop-bar lineup over to Masi in 2025.
items.lbText:
Haro Bikes, a legacy BMX brand, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. BRAIN has reported that the California-based brand made the filing on Tuesday morning.

The petition was signed by Bjarke Rasmussen, the CEO of Haro, and comes after a year of financial strain for the brand following its entry into the drop-bar market.

Ultimately, the weight of a mounting disparity between its assets and liabilities put the Haro brand under legal pressure as Kenstone, a major bike assembler in Taiwan, sued the brand in 2024 for $2.86 million worth of unpaid product.

In response to that lawsuit, Rasmussen told BRAIN that tariff policy and headwinds in the US bike market had challenged the brand domestically. The brand also cut its US staff by one-third in October of last year.

For the drop-bar bike world, Haro is already a road and gravel brand that is resigned to the dustbin of history. The Haro Rivette road bike now sits as a blip in the brand’s history, as Masi, a legacy name in road cycling history, replaced Haro as the company’s brand for all drop-bar bikes in 2025.

While sources close to the company have said plans for future Haro and Masi bikes will continue into the new year, Chapter 11 bankruptcy will undoubtedly lead to further battles in court between Haro and its debtors.

For more on the Haro bankruptcy and what it means for the brand moving forward, check out the full story on BRAIN .

items.title: Scott Sports Details Popemobile-Inspired E-Bike Built for Pope Leo XIV
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The Swiss brand paired a step-through SUB Tour 10 Wave and Sierra MIPS helmet with a papal crest, building on its UCI Solidarity Program tie.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Scott Sports provided a custom electric bicycle to Pope Leo XIV during Monday’s UCI-organized audience at the Vatican, with the Swiss company sharing details today on the tailored build. According to Scott, the bike and helmet carry a marble-white and silver scheme inspired by the Popemobile, while the helmet also features a subtle papal crest on the front.

According to Scott, the build pairs a step-through SUB Tour 10 Wave urban e-bike with a matching Sierra MIPS helmet. The presentation extends Scott’s longstanding partnership with the UCI World Cycling Centre in Aigle, Switzerland, where the brand supplies most of the road and mountain bikes distributed to developing athletes and national federations through the UCI Solidarity Program.

Designed for everyday urban riding rather than performance racing, the SUB Tour 10 Wave uses a low-step frame, internal belt drive, suspension fork, integrated lights, fenders, and a rear rack. Scott did not disclose any mechanical modifications to the motor or drivetrain, keeping the bespoke changes centered on the finish and styling.

The presentation took place inside the Vatican’s Clementine Hall, where roughly 100 past and present cyclists—including Eddy Merckx, Greg LeMond, and Demi Vollering—attended a gathering organized by the UCI and the Vatican’s Dicastery for Culture and Education. As Velo reported Monday, UCI President David Lappartient presented a signed rainbow jersey reading “Leone XIV,” while Vincenzo Nibali and Vollering handed over signed Grand Tour leader jerseys.

items.title: This Smart Trainer Takes Indoor Training to the Next Level
items.author: Emily LaPointe
items.content: Elite’s new Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click brings the popular virtual cycling technology to the most advanced riders
items.lbText:
The Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click (Photo: Elite)

When you can’t get out for a ride—whether it’s snowy, hot, smoky, or cold, or you just don’t have the time—indoor training fills in the gaps. The right training equipment keeps your workouts consistent and your fitness gains on track, no matter what’s going on outside. And with the right smart trainer, at-home rides can even be—dare we say it?—fun.

Italian cycling brand Elite has been at the forefront of training technology for nearly 50 years, developing smart trainers and bike accessories for all levels of cyclists. Elite’s latest innovation, the Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click , brings the brand’s signature accuracy, responsiveness, and realistic ride feel to a top-of-the-line product for the most serious cyclists.

The Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click Elite

The standard Justo 2 is the smart trainer of choice for some of the best racing teams in the world: UAE Team Emirates XRG, France’s Groupama-FDJ UNITED, and the Netherlands’ PICNIC PostNL. The specs speak for themselves: a power meter that’s accurate within 1 percent, automatic resistance control up to 24 percent, built-in WiFi as well as ANT+FE-C and Bluetooth, and high-speed data transmission. And with two different types of Flex Feet, you can conform your trainer to your personal pedaling style for a more realistic feel.

The Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click adds the Zwift Ready configuration to this flagship design. Zwift Cog comes preinstalled, so all you need to do is mount your 8-to-13-speed bike and start pedaling—no cassette to fiddle with, no derailleur adjustment, no worries about compatibility. Zwift Click finishes the setup by putting Zwift virtual shifting right on the handlebars, so you can easily shift 24 silent gears, navigate menus, and steer. The Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click connects straight to your home network and updates automatically, leaving you free to concentrate on workouts and races.

With the addition of the Justo 2 with Zwift Cog and Click to the line, Elite now offers a Zwift-ready system for every level. The Rivo is the accessible, entry-level smart trainer, while the Avanti represents a step up in intensity. Now, the highest-level cyclists can also click into the challenge, competition, and fun of the industry’s leading virtual training program.

Founded in 1979, Elite develops products for training, racing, and everyday riding. Known worldwide for its bottles, cages, and indoor training technologies, Elite is one of the most represented suppliers in the WorldTour peloton, developing and testing products at the highest level of the sport. Discover more on elite-it.com .

items.title: USA Crits Expands to Virginia, Brings Back a Seven Race Series for 2027
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The series adds Newport News Twilight to its lineup of criteriums around the American Southeast in a seven-race, three-week block.
items.lbText:
One of the two major American criterium series has announced its 2027 lineup, with USA Crits adding the Newport News Twilight Criterium in Virginia to kick off the series.

The 2027 series will have seven races packed into a three-week block of racing throughout the Southeast between April 10th and May 1st. As always, the biggest draw from the series will be the marquee event of Athens Twilight. Athens Twilight, or Twilight as it is known locally in Athens, is a fundamental race on the American calendar.

Not only has the race been around for decades, but it has also been a local institution as well, serving as a celebration of the end of the school year at the University of Georgia on the final week of classes. It is equal parts bike race and festival that anchors the race to the community. From that strength, USA Crits has been a multi-decade-long attempt to extend that success to more events across the Southeast.

“When we started Athens Twilight in 1980, the idea was simple: bring great bike racing to the people. USA Crits was built on that same philosophy,” Gene Dixon, Founder of USA Crits and Athens Twilight, said in a press release. “Nearly 20 years after launching the series, we’re still bringing the best riders in the country to communities that embrace the excitement of professional cycling.”

All the races in the series will be live-streamed and will combine amateur racing with the fastest criterium racers in the US. In tandem with the American Criterium Cup, known as the ACC, the two series make up the bulk of American crit racing. While USA Crits occupies spring, the ACC claims the summer, with races throughout the West and Midwest.

items.title: Egan Bernal Isn’t Done Yet as Netcompany-Ineos Continues Its 2027 Reboot
items.author: ahood
items.content: No retirement for Egan Bernal. The former Tour de France winner re-ups his contract as Netcompany-Ineos navigates another winter of big changes.
items.lbText:
Bernal signed a contract extension with Netcompany-Ineos. (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images)

Egan Bernal isn’t ready to hang up his wheels just yet.

The 2019 Tour de France winner signed a contract extension with Netcompany-Ineos to squelch any retirement rumors as well as give the British team some continuity in what’s another season of major roster changes.

Bernal, who turns 30 in January, shot down suggestions this summer that he was considering retirement when his current deal expired at the end of 2026.

The team confirmed Tuesday that Bernal will race on in team colors, but did not reveal the length or terms of the new deal. Unconfirmed reports suggest the Colombian superstar has signed on for another three seasons.

“This team has been my home since 2018 and has supported me through the best moments of my career and the hardest ones,” Bernal said Tuesday. “After a break to recharge, I’m coming back with a clear head and looking forward to building towards next season with the team.

“I know what I’m capable of and I still believe I have a lot to give. I want to enjoy the racing and help this group achieve something special in the seasons ahead.”

Bernal remains the last rider to win the Tour for the British squad, and the last rider not named Tadej Pogačar or Jonas Vingegaard to win the yellow jersey.

The Colombian backed up his 2019 Tour victory by winning the 2021 Giro d’Italia before a horrific training crash in January 2022 nearly ended his career .

Bernal has clawed his way back , finishing seventh and 10th in the past two editions of the Giro, but he’s yet to rediscover the diamonds in his legs that once made him the most exciting young GC racer in the peloton.

Bernal’s contract extension comes at an interesting crossroads for the British team in 2027 as Geraint Thomas enters his second season in top management.

The loss of French petrochemical giant TotalEnergies as a major financial partner comes on the heels of an injury-plagued 2026 campaign that delivered some wins, but saw the team far from the conversation in the fight for the yellow jersey in a bad-luck campaign this summer.

The other grand tours went better, with Thymen Arensman fourth at the Giro and Oscar Onley sixth at the Vuelta. It team ended 2026 eighth in the UCI team rankings.

“Egan’s a huge part of this team,” Thomas said. “What he’s come back from and what he’s achieved since is just unreal. He’s a champion in every sense of the word. The younger riders look up to him and they can learn a lot from his determination and the way he goes about things, on and off the bike. The whole team is really happy he’s staying.”

Bernal’s contract extension comes in a major makeover for Netcompany-Ineos, the team that once ruled the Tour de France in the 2010s, with seven yellow jerseys in eight years from four different riders.

Nine new riders arrive for 2027, headlined by Spanish junior world champion Benjamín Noval and promising British talent Joseph Blackmore, a Tour de l’Avenir winner in 2024.

Michael Valgren, Markel Beloki, James Shaw, Clément Champoussin, Harold Tejada, Javier Romo, and American sprinter Riley Sheehan round out the incoming transfers .

There’s arguably more star power going out the door than coming in.

Filippo Ganna, Ben Turner, Laurens De Plus, Sam Welsford, Victor Langellotti and Americans Magnus Sheffield, Andrew August, and Artem Shmidt are all swapping teams , while veterans Ben Swift and Bob Jungels both retire.

Bernal didn’t outline his top ambitions for 2027, but it seems like his Tour GC aspirations are a page from the past.

A win during a protest-shortened stage at the 2025 Vuelta a España is his only major European victory since his 2022 crash.

The team is banking on a healthy Onley — its marquee signing last winter who missed out on the Tour de France this summer due to injury — will be back in top condition. A promising sixth and the best young rider’s jersey at the Vuelta is a good sign.

What’s missing from the Netcompany-Ineos class of 2027 is a blockbuster GC signing that might elbow the team back into the Tour de France conversation.

That’s fueling some speculation that management is keeping its powder dry for a possible run at French sensation Paul Seixas , whose contract with Decathlon-CMA CGM expires at the end of 2027.

items.title: 500 Miles on Mosaic’s New 32″ Shows How Big Wheels Can Unlock Gravel’s Full Potential
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: From racing Big Sugar to riding loose desert switchbacks, Mosaic’s GT i55 32 is the first bike to prove 32-inch wheels can challenge the status quo.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Better traction, regardless of tire Aggressive front end that makes the bike feel nimble Balanced handling and great weight distribution A conventional fit that feels natural despite the wheel size

Heavy vs comparable 700c bikes One fork configuration leads to some wonky geometry with smaller-sized frames Slack seat tube angles can be challenging for some modern fits Limited bag, rack, and water bottle attachments for longer adventures

Weight: 21.6 pounds (9.79 kilos), ready to ride, without pedals

Price: $14,700 for the GT-1 i55 32, with upgraded Duke Sierra 42 wheelset.

While Mosaic’s nascent entry into the 32-inch gravel world is a truly unique ride experience, it quite plainly shows how 32-inch wheels are emphatically better on gravel and worse on pavement. Much is yet to come, but from several hundred miles of riding across tons of different terrain, I can confidently say the Mosiac GT i55 32 is good enough to challenge the status quo.

We have been excited for this bike review for a long time. Ever since the build-up to Sea Otter, what was clear was that 32-inch gravel bikes were coming. We didn’t know when, and we didn’t know exactly what they would look like, but by the end of the year we knew there would be bikes to test with a new wheel size.

Well, folks, here we are. After hundreds of miles After hundreds of miles of riding the Mosaic GT i55 32, we have Velo ’s first full long-term review of a 32-inch gravel race bike.

Since we got the bike in early October, we have thrown everything at the bike. Long mostly-paved days riding on the East Coast, short punchy gravel races in the Midwest, and twisty gravel trail rides in the Southwest—all of it to see just how viable the first 32-inch gravel bike to hit the market can handle all these different gravel challenges. In the end, we were blown away by just how ready the wheel size already seems for the right type of rider.

The Mosaic GT i55 32 frame is defined by two distinct, but equally important parts. On one hand is the carbon fork, produced by Mosaic’s new sister brand Zero Components; on the other, a built-in Colorado titanium frame. Together, the two components create the customizable basis for the bike with a set front end and an adjustable rear. That flexibility has allowed Mosaic to be the first brand to bring a true purpose-built 32-inch gravel bike to market.

As we covered when the bike was released, the fork is crucially important for that speed to market. Before Zero Components launched its 32-inch fork in conjunction with the GT i55 32, most 32-inch prototypes relied upon existing 29-inch mountain bike forks. Those forks had very large axle-to-crown figures, which meant the bikes had to have tall front ends and slack head tube angles.

The Zero Components fork transformed that calculus with a significantly shorter axle-to-crown figure. This unlocked the geometry of the titanium frame to more closely resemble that of 700c bikes, and for the resulting handling to feel more natural and responsive.

That said, the rest of the bike also demanded its own solutions to the fit and geometry problems posed by the new larger wheels. Namely, how long the chainstays and how low the bottom bracket would be to fit around three more inches of wheel and the same large tire clearance.

Ultimately, Mosaic did not totally address all of those concerns at first with the announcement of the new bike. Mosaic is a brand that has long built custom frames. This is a foundational aspect of the brand, so it is not a surprise that the brand only offered custom geometry in the first run of 32-inch bikes.

What that meant, though, was no overall geometry chart showing what a smaller 32-inch gravel bike would look like—the enduring concern around the new wheel size. All we got were the parameters around chainstay lengths that would stay between 440-450 mm, and the design language of a kinked seat tube that would allow for a small rear triangle that could fit around the bigger wheel. That bent seat tube could make some saddle positions tough to reach, since the shallower angle can push higher saddle positions further behind the bottom bracket.

Now, that has changed with Mosaic combining custom geometry with a standard layout to build around. The GT-1 premium build uses custom geometry, but Mosaic does have standard geometry it uses as the basis of those builds. It also comes standard with the GT-2. While the standard chainstay length of 450mm and bottom bracket drop of 95mm are much bigger than 700c gravel bikes, the overall reach, stack, and angles throughout the bike aren’t too revolutionary.

In particular, the 69-71 degree headtube with a fork offset of 60mm does make for pretty conventional dimensions. The one obvious outlier here is the 50cm frame size having a trail figure of 88, which is pushing the limits of normal gravel bike ride feel. For the 56cm frame, the fit parameters of a 70.5 head tube, 60mm offset, and 408mm of reach are all very familiar to progressive gravel bikes.

I ended up testing a 56cm frame even though I fluctuate between 56 and 58cm for different bike geometries. With a 56cm frame, the fit ended up being virtually the same as what I currently ride with a Specialized Crux 5 56cm frame, with the major difference being a 90mm stem and wider bars on the Mosaic and a 120mm stem with narrower bars on the Specialized.…

items.title: Decathlon Goes All In on ‘Project Seixas’ to Convince French Superstar to Stay
items.author: ahood
items.content: Decathlon hires DS Winston and signs O'Connor, Sivakov in latest moves to build a super team around Paul Seixas before his contract expires at the end of 2027.
items.lbText:
Decathlon is doing everything it can to keep Seixas beyond 2027. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Decathlon-CMA CGM is pulling out all the stops to keep Paul Seixas on board.

With a blockbuster bidding war looming for the French phenom’s signature, Decathlon is quietly building a super team around Seixas in the hope of making it almost impossible for him to walk away.

The ambitious French WorldTour team added another piece to the puzzle with the arrival of veteran British sports director Matt Winston in its latest move to build a Tour de France-winning machine around Seixas and convince him to stay beyond 2027 .

Winston joins from Picnic PostNL to reunite with former rider Romain Bardet, who is taking on a senior management role as the money-rich French team undergoes another dramatic winter rebuild.

“His arrival fully reflects our desire to keep developing an ambitious, internationally minded project, which was a decisive factor in his decision to join us,” Bardet said Tuesday. “His experience in supporting both sprinters and general classification leaders is a real asset for our team”

With Seixas out of contract at the end of 2027 and rival super teams circling, Decathlon is moving aggressively on several fronts to create the sporting, technical, and financial infrastructure to keep its prized asset.

The stakes for Decathlon couldn’t be higher.

With the backing of a pair of French multinational sponsors, the team has the money, and it’s been spending it going into 2027.

Every move is designed to convince Seixas, 20, to remain in team kit beyond this season.

“Paul is going to win with us,” Decathlon general manager Dominique Serieys told Le Parisien after the 2026 Tour. “He’s already won big races with us and we’re going to keep making the team stronger so we’re better than the others. And regardless of any new contract, in three or four years, he’ll only be 23 or 24.”

Seixas confirmed the hype in 2026 with one of the most spectacular teenage campaigns in modern cycling history, with victories at Il Lombardia, La Flèche Wallonne, and Itzulia Basque Country, and fourth overall in his Tour de France debut.

Serieys now has the job to convince France’s best candidate to win the yellow jersey since Bernard Hinault last won in 1985 to stay with the French-backed squad.

With UAE Emirates-XRG and Visma-Lease a Bike looming with mega-deals that could make Seixas one of the best-paid riders in the peloton , Decathlon brass know they cannot take anything for granted.

The arrival of two-time podium finisher Bardet as team manager will give Seixas a direct French-speaking mentor who knows the pressure to be named as France’s “next great hope.”

Decathlon also spent in the transfer market to build up its climbing corps to create a solid grand tour mountain train around Seixas.

New arrivals Ben O’Connor, back to his former team, Pavel Sivakov, and Laurens De Plus bring legs and experience.

Alongside American rider Matthew Riccitello, Léo Bisiaux, and Nicolas Prodhomme, Seixas will know he will have support in the grand tours.

The departures of Felix Gall and Gregor Mühlberger, both to Lidl-Trek, also signal this is his team if Seixas wants it.

Decathlon also shifted its legal registration to Switzerland, a move that could provide greater financial flexibility when it comes to taxes and social fees that would come with any blockbuster deal.

So far, the Frenchman isn’t giving much away about his long-term future.

“I haven’t made a decision yet,” Seixas told RMC Radio in October. “When you look at how the team has developed, it’s not even the same team compared to last year.”

Seixas came up through the ranks with Decathlon, racing on its development team before winning the Tour de l’Avenir in 2025 and making the jump to the WorldTour squad.

Right now, even his 2027 racing calendar remains undecided.

One option making the rounds is a tilt at winning the Giro d’Italia , potentially skipping the Tour de France to target the world championships on home roads in Sallanches, where Hinault famously won the rainbow jersey in 1980.

Sooner or later, he will have to decide.

There’s huge pressure inside France for him to stay on a French team, so Decathlon is pulling out all the stops to try build a team that could rival the UAE’s and Visma’s of the peloton.

Winston arrivals also makes him part of an increasingly international backroom staff that already includes Luke Rowe, Luke Roberts, and Mark Renshaw.

Bardet will report directly to Serieys as sports manager to help steer the team’s broader sporting strategy. A women’s team is also being rolled out in 2027 as the team’s ambitions — and budget — grows.

Winston spent eight seasons at Picnic PostNL, working with the team’s sprinters and GC contenders, including Bardet.

“I’m looking forward to new challenges and a new way of working, and I’m confident there are many more great races to come,” Winston said.”I’ll be focused on working with the other sports directors and the management to help the team perform at the highest level, with big ambitions. It’s an international team and I can’t wait to get started.”

Whether Seixas is part of the team beyond 2027 remains TBD.
